summary: Updates RFC 8410 to clarify existing semantics and add missing ones for the key usage bits in certificates supporting the Ed25519, Ed448, X25519, and X448 elliptic curve algorithms. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: A certificate says what a key may be used for, like signing or locking. This clears up confusing wording for four modern key types so everyone reads the labels the same way.

questions: what key usage bits should ed25519 certificates have
how to set key usage for x25519 certificates
which bits are forbidden for elliptic curve keys
subtitle: Clarifies key usage bits for modern elliptic curve algorithms in certificates.

tldr.problem: RFC 8410 defined four modern elliptic curve algorithms (Ed25519, Ed448, X25519, X448) but left unclear which key usage bits should appear in their certificates.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9295 adds explicit rules for what key usage bits must, may, or must not be present depending on the certificate type (end-entity, certification authority, or CRL issuer) and algorithm.
tldr.outcome: Certificate implementations and validators now have clear guidance, ensuring consistent handling of these signature and key agreement algorithms across the Internet.

today: RFC 9295 is the current standard defining key usage for these modern algorithms. All certificate software should follow its rules when issuing or validating certificates with Ed25519, Ed448, X25519, or X448 keys.

sections.title: Modern Elliptic Curve Keys
sections.content:
RFC 8410 introduced four elliptic curve cryptography algorithms: Ed25519 and Ed448 for signing, and X25519 and X448 for key agreement (secure handshakes). These are now widely used in certificates, but RFC 8410 was unclear about which key usage bits should appear on certificates for each algorithm.

Key usage bits are a standard way to label what a key is allowed to do: sign documents, verify other certificates, decrypt data, or agree on shared secrets. Without clear rules, implementations disagreed.
sections.plainLanguage: Keys have permission labels. Modern keys can sign, or they can agree on secrets. The old rules didn't clearly say which labels each key type needs.

sections.title: Key Usage Rules
sections.content:
For X25519 and X448 (key agreement): the keyAgreement bit MUST be present. The bits encipherOnly and decipherOnly MAY also appear, but signing-related bits like digitalSignature and keyCertSign MUST NOT.

For Ed25519 and Ed448 signing keys, the rules depend on the certificate's role. End-entity certificates MUST have at least one of nonRepudiation, digitalSignature, or cRLSign, and MUST NOT have key-agreement bits. Certification authority certificates MUST have keyCertSign. CRL issuer certificates (which sign revocation lists) MUST have cRLSign.
sections.plainLanguage: If a key does key agreement, it must be labeled for that and nothing else. If a key signs, it gets signing labels, and the exact labels depend on what role the certificate plays.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content: These clarifications prevent misuse of keys. By enforcing that a key agreement key cannot also be used for signing, and vice versa, the RFC reduces the risk of a key being used for an unintended purpose. The separation between signing keys and key-agreement keys is fundamental to modern cryptography.
sections.plainLanguage: Keeping key permissions simple and clear prevents accidents. A key that does one job well is safer than a key that tries to do everything.

references.text: Josefsson, S. and J. Schaad, "Algorithm Identifiers for Ed25519, Ed448, X25519, and X448 for Use in the Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure", RFC 8410, DOI 10.17487/RFC8410, August 2018.
